The final F3 task was taking project approaches and developing a toolkit that could guide smaller communities in replicating F3 project planning approaches and resilience analysis. Completion of the final milestone included creating the toolkit methodology, incorporating best practices for community engagement, and amplifying the Duluth approach. The City of Duluth worked with staff from three other Midwest communities to review and test F3 approaches. 9 Project Results and Discussion Tasks were initially ordered in the Statement of Performance Objectives based upon the timing of the milestones. This meant that the asset-based planning work was completed as part of Task 1.0 and Task 3.0, separated by the concurrent community-based bottom-up planning. For reporting results, it is clearer to discuss all asset-based work together. Hazards Analysis and Disruption Scenarios • Development of 8 grid disruption scenarios. • Resilient power siting criteria rubric designed. • 10 prioritized sites for resilient power development determined. Task 3.0 Milestone • Top-Down Asset-based Energy Resilience • Prioritized site analysis report completed. Planning Although Duluth has been named a “climate refuge” city in popular media, in 2012, heavy storms caused unprecedented flooding along the St. Louis River, causing severe damage. In 2016, a derecho 250 miles in length led to power loss for 75,000 of Minnesota Power’s customers. In 2018, 60mph winds caused a storm surge that cost $18.4 million in recovery and mitigation efforts. Because of these, and other extreme weather events, the City of Duluth instituted a Climate Action Work Plan (CAWP) in 2022 after declaring a climate emergency in 2021. Two priorities in the CAWP, including driving down emissions from City operations and strengthening community resilience, were advanced by Duluth’s RACER approach. It was recognized that in order to advance community resilience, a thoughtful asset-based approach needed to be informed by rigorous and authentic community engagement. Figure 2. Five-year CAIDI reliability map for Duluth, MN, used to understand overall grid performance and help identify any areas that could use additional resilience investment (Appendix A). 10 The first step under F3 was to convene a Critical Infrastructure Team (CIT). A group of 12 individuals across 6 City departments and 3 partner organizations were brought together to determine outage scenarios with differing disaster contexts that ranged from previously experienced outages to events with cascading failures. With participation by Minnesota Power, the IOU utility that provides electricity to the region, the CIT examined existing blue-sky grid reliability metrics including five-year Customer Average Interruption Duration Index (CAIDI) (Figure 2), System Average Interruption Duration Index (SAIDI), and System Average Interruption Frequency Index (SAIFI) data for feeders serving Duluth. Because CAIDI data often excludes storms, the CIT included information (below- Figure 3) on all events for the preceding 5-years.
